claims.text: Repetitive mechanical disruption of a passive film, together with the rate of re-passivation, governs total tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys.
When passive-film removal outpaces film regrowth, the wear rate increases.
When passive-film removal outpaces film regrowth, the corrosion rate increases and produces synergistic damage.
The starting high-entropy alloy has a stable passive film in a chloride-containing environment.
The starting high-entropy alloy has moderate hardness.
Normal load, sliding speed, and electrochemical potential can be varied systematically in one tribo-corrosion cell while monitoring mechanical loss, electrochemical response, and re-passivation.
A surface oxide or passive layer is protective against environmental degradation.
Continuous mechanical disruption of the surface layer changes local corrosion kinetics through de-passivation and re-passivation cycles.
Higher mechanical load or contact pressure causes more frequent passive-film breakdown.
Rapid oxide regrowth limits corrosion between successive sliding events.
The balance between film-disruption rate and re-passivation kinetics determines the magnitude of synergistic wear-corrosion damage.
Higher normal loads will increase total tribo-corrosion mass loss.
Faster sliding speeds will increase total tribo-corrosion mass loss.
Under sufficiently high loads and sliding speeds, combined mass loss will exceed the sum of separately measured pure-corrosion and pure-wear losses.
Increasing re-passivation kinetics will reduce tribo-corrosion synergy and overall degradation.
Separate pure-corrosion and inert-environment pure-wear tests provide an additive baseline for identifying synergy.
Synergy should be negligible in extremely inert environments or at loads too low to disrupt the passive film appreciably.
At very high loads or in extremely aggressive solutions, large-scale plastic deformation or localized corrosion may dominate over the proposed film-kinetics mechanism.
Microcracking, microstructural variation, and compositional variation can alter re-passivation behavior and confound the predicted synergy.
If changing film re-passivation speed at fixed load and sliding speed does not change measured synergy, the proposed governing role of re-passivation kinetics is falsified.
